newsitem.title: KENYA: Tanzania's flower growers report rapid growth.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania's flower growers report rapid growth.

text.p: Tanzania's young horticultural industry in the northern highlands surrounding Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Meru has taken off on a development track, growers and farm analysts said on Tuesday.
In recent years output has doubled and exports of cut flowers to European markets are now increasing almost daily.
Industry officials see Tanzania as a major player in the global flower market in the near future.
The area under cultivation around Arusha and Moshi has grown to 70 hectares (173 acres) from only 40 as recently as 10 months ago.

With a jump from one grower in the early 1990s to six companies now, and another four waiting to start cultivation, they expect the cultivated area to increase to more than 100 hectares by the end of this year.
"It's getting more and more competitive here. Now there is about 70 hectares of flowers, but all the companies are expanding," said Adrian Moss, estate manager for Hortanzia Ltd.

Hortanzia, backed by private Tanzanian and Kenyan investment, started business in 1993 with just two hectares and seven greenhouses. Its business has already expanded to five hectares and 13 greenhouses.

Heikki Niskala, farm manager for the biggest of the growers, Kiliflora Ltd, said the industry would continue to expand and it was likely that Tanzania would, within the next five to 10 years, become one of the biggest producers in Africa.
"We ship in terms of weight 25 to 30 tonnes a week of flowers. In terms of stems we are looking at close to a million stems a week," Niskala told Reuters.

Kiliflora grows only roses, mostly of the varieties known as First Red, Baroness and Escada, at the company's farm of 18 hectares. Cultivation on a new 12-hectare farm is expected to start by the beginning of next season in mid-August.
"Within three years from now the plan is to reach 50 hectares and by that time Kiliflora will become one of the biggest rose plantations in all of Africa," he said.
While Kiliflora has concentrated on roses, increasingly in demand in Europe, Hortanzia has started experiments with the flower variety lizianthus.
The growers' optimism is echoed in the world's biggest flower auctions in the Netherlands, which see East Africa, and especially Tanzania, as an increasingly important source of high quality flowers.

"Tanzania has the potential. The Kilimanjaro area is excellent for the growing of flowers and there is quite some development coming up in the Arusha region at the moment," said Feico Smit, Africa area manager of Bloemen Veiling Holland.

"...Next season we are going to focus on the markets in Tanzania and Zambia which we will provide with advice and support," said Albert Haasnoot, direct sales account manager of Bloemen Veiling Flora, with an annual turnover of $390 million.

German importer Omniflora is so optimistic about the potential of Tanzania's flower industry that the company has initiated an agreement with a private freight company in Nairobi to start chartered cargo flights to Kilimanjaro.
Two-thirds of the production from Tanzania is exported to the Dutch flower auctions in Amsterdam while the remaining third goes mostly to Frankfurt.
Flower exports now earn Tanzania around $10 million a year in hard currency earnings, but exporters see that amount increasing.
